name: Ems-Weser Frisian
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Fort, Marron C. (2001) Das Saterfriesische, in Handbuch des Friesischen; Slofstra, Hoekstra & Leppers (2021) Grammatik des Saterfriesischen

new_statements.quote: Specifically, a phonological word in Saterland Frisian can consist of one of the following: (i) a lexical stem, which may be extended by (a) prefixes with a reduced vowel, (b) the prefix /bi/, or (c) suffixes that begin with a vowel; (ii) a prefix with a full vowel (except /bi/); and (iii) a suffix that has a full vowel and begins with a consonant. Morphological words comprise one or more phonological words. In morphological words comprising a single phonological word the primary word stress falls on the last stressed syllable. If they comprise more than one phonological word, the primary word stress falls on the last stressed syllable of the first phonological word.
new_statements.citation: Peters, Jörg. 2019. Saterland Frisian (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 49(2): 223-230. doi:10.1017/S0025100317000226 (first published online 15 June 2017). Open access.
new_statements.locator: section 'Word stress and intonation', pp. 228-229 (pdf pp. 6-7)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: the full passage ("Specifically, a phonological word in Saterland Frisian can consist of one of the following: (i) a lexical stem... the primary word stress falls on the last stressed syllable of the first phonological word.") is present verbatim (line breaks aside) in lines 292-299; extracted text on the PDF puts the section heading "Word stress and intonation" on PDF page 6 and its continuation (with the running head "Jörg Peters: Saterland Frisian 229") on PDF page 7, so the locator pp. 228-229 / PDF pp. 6-7 is right. Surrounding section read: it also gives the six-word illustration table (/ˈtumə/, /zəˈlɔːt/, /biˈprɔːljə/, /ˈutˌdrɪŋkə/, /ˈdɪskdɔu̯k/, /ˌeːləˈfant/), the Fort…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is morphologically/prosodically governed, on the German model (Peters follows Wiese 2000): a phonological word is a lexical stem plus any schwa-prefixes, the prefix bi-, and vowel-initial suffixes; full-vowel prefixes (except bi-) and consonant-initial full-vowel suffixes form their own phonological words. Within a single phonological word primary stress goes on its last stressable (full-vowel) syllable — in practice the stem, since schwa cannot bear stress (/ˈtumə/ 'thumb', /biˈprɔːljə/ 'to praise'); in loans this yields final stress (/zəˈlɔːt/ 'salad', /ˌeːləˈfant/ 'elephant'). In words of more than one phonological word (particle verbs, compounds) primary stress is on the last stressed syllable of the FIRST phonological word (/ˈutˌdrɪŋkə/ 'to drink up', /ˈdɪskdɔu̯k/ 'tablecloth'). The Sprachlehre des Saterfriesischen (Slofstra & Hoekstra 2023: 97-98) agrees for verbs: separable verb particles are stressed (AN-aaskje), inseparable prefix verbs stress the stem (be-fläkke).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated as a rule; secondary stress is marked in the examples on the non-initial phonological word of compounds (/ˈutˌdrɪŋkə/) and on the initial full-vowel syllable of loans (/ˌeːləˈfant/, ˌäärmˈzoalig, ˌstjúurˈfräi).
new_statements.exceptions: Peters (citing Fort 2015) lists compounds borrowed from Northern Standard German with stress on the second element, unlike their German cognates: Sfrs. ˌäärmˈzoalig vs. Nsg. ˈarmˌselig 'miserable', lichtˈfäidig vs. ˈleichtˌfertig 'careless', ˌstjúurˈfräi vs. ˈsteuerˌfrei 'tax-free' — explained as the loans being treated as single phonological words whose last stressed syllable attracts primary stress. Also: 'In today's language, there is no clear indication of a word accent distinction between GESTOSSENER TON ('push tone') and GESCHLIFFENER TON ('dragging tone'), as assumed by Siebs (1889) for the Saterland Frisian of his time.' Stress rules apply to loans too. Slofstra & Hoekstra note variable stress in a few prefix verbs (mis-gunge / MISS-gunge; truch-ÖILE / TRUCH-öile) and a stress-distinguished pair uur-slo 'not heed' vs UUR-slo 'get warm'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (morphological word made of one or more phonological words, incl. compounds and particle verbs); based on citation-form elicitation and recorded passage from three elderly trilingual speakers (Ramsloh, Scharrel, Strücklingen). Intonation is said to match Northern Standard German. Classification as 'morphological-root' is my mapping: stress is stem/prosodic-word-determined, not position-counted or weight-based; 'fixed-final' would fit only loans/simplex words read as 'last full-vowel syllable'.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog's sate1242 'Ems-Weser Frisian' bundles living Saterland Frisian (Ems Frisian; dialects of Ramsloh, Strücklingen, Scharrel/Sedelsberg) with the extinct Weser Frisian of Wangerooge/Wursten (Glottolog refs Ehrentraut 1849-54, Versloot 2001, Siebs 1954, Gregersen 2023 are Wangeroogic). The statement quoted is for Saterland Frisian only (Peters 2019, three speakers from Ramsloh, Scharrel, Strücklingen). Taalportaal's Saterfrisian introduction notes that Old Weser Frisian differed: 'in some words, the main accent fell on the second syllable, with reduction of the first one' (kma 'come', snu 'son'; citing Versloot 2001a,b) — so the Wangerooge variety should not be assumed to share the Saterland pattern.

sources.note: Ch. 1 'Schreibweise und Aussprache' (pp. 15-24) gives no general word-stress rule (only that /ə/ is 'der meistens unbetonte Vokal', p. 16). Stress remarks in morphology: 'Der Verbzusatz wird betont (AN-aaskje, iek aaskje AN)' (p. 97) and 'Andere Verben werden mit einem Präfix zusammengesetzt. Der Verbalstamm wird betont, also: be-fläkke' (p. 98), with variants mis-gunge/MISS-gunge, truch-ÖILE/TRUCH-öile and the pair uur-slo vs UUR-slo; stressed vs unstressed pronoun forms (pp. 60-61, 86ff).

sources.citation: Peters, Jörg. 2019. Saterland Frisian (Illustrations of the IPA). JIPA 49(2): 223-230. doi:10.1017/S0025100317000226.
sources.note: pp. 228-229 'Word stress and intonation': primary stress on the last stressed syllable of the (first) phonological word, defined à la Wiese 2000 (stem + schwa-prefixes + bi- + vowel-initial suffixes); loans obey the same rule; German-loan compounds with deviant final-element stress; no push/dragging-tone accent distinction today (contra Siebs 1889).
